sources.entry: Intel Memory Latency Checker - Measures the node-to-node latency and bandwidth matrix and loaded latency on the x86 at hand, which no datasheet states.

summary.title: Intel® Memory Latency Checker v3.12
summary.one_liner: Intel MLC is a command-line tool that measures memory latency and bandwidth on x86 systems, including how latency rises under increasing load, NUMA node-to-node matrices, and cache-to-cache transfers.
keywords: how to measure memory latency on linux
takeaways: Running mlc with no arguments prints an idle latency matrix, peak bandwidth by read/write mix, a bandwidth matrix, and latency at different bandwidth points.
Load-generation threads inject increasing traffic while a single latency thread runs dependent pointer-chase reads, showing how latency changes with load.
MLC disables hardware prefetchers during tests, which requires root on Linux (the msr module must be loaded) unless run with the -e option.
Command-line options such as --latency_matrix, --bandwidth_matrix, --loaded_latency, --c2c_latency and --memory_bandwidth_scan select specific measurements.
summary.summary: This Intel Developer article documents the Intel Memory Latency Checker (MLC) v3.12 tool. It explains what the tool measures (idle latency matrices across sockets, peak and max bandwidth for read/write mixes, latency versus bandwidth load, and cache-to-cache transfers), and how it works: load-generation threads throttle traffic while one latency thread runs dependent reads. It covers Linux and Windows installation, the need for root access to control hardware prefetchers, the main command-line options, and a version changelog from 1.0 through 3.13. The page lists new features but does not include usage examples or sample output beyond what is described.
